title: Βροντὴ καὶ κλεηδών
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, lying awake in the vestibule, prays to Zeus for two signs: a chance word from someone waking in the house, and a portent from Zeus outside. Zeus thunders at once, and one of the twelve women grinding meal at the mills, weakest and last to stop, hears it, calls it a portent and prays that the suitors may feast today for the last time; Odysseus rejoices at the omen. The household stirs. Telemachus dresses, arms himself and asks Eurycleia whether the stranger has been given bed and food; she answers that he drank his wine, said he wanted no more food, and himself refused a bed. Telemachus goes off to the assembly with two dogs, and Eurycleia sets the maids to sweeping, cleaning and fetching water, because the suitors will be back early for a festival. Then the herdsmen come in. Eumaeus brings hogs and asks Odysseus how the Achaeans now treat him; Odysseus wishes the gods would punish them. Melanthius brings goats and taunts him, and Odysseus answers only with a shake of the head. Philoetius brings a cow and goats, asks who the stranger is, and greets him with his right hand.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, εἴ μ’ ἐθέλοντες ἐπὶ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρὴν
ἤγετ’ ἐμὴν ἐς γαῖαν, ἐπεί μ’ ἐκακώσατε λίην,
φήμην τίς μοι φάσθω ἐγειρομένων ἀνθρώπων
ἔνδοθεν, ἔκτοσθεν δὲ Διὸς τέρας ἄλλο φανήτω.
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater, ei m’ ethelontes epi trapherēn te kai hygrēn
ēget’ emēn es gaian, epei m’ ekakōsate liēn,
phēmēn tis moi phasthō egeiromenōn anthrōpōn
endothen, ektosthen de Dios teras allo phanētō.
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, if willing you over both the solid and the wet
led me to my own land, since you have afflicted me greatly,
a saying let someone speak to me, of men who are waking,
from within, and outside let another portent of Zeus appear.”
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, if you gods were willing to bring me over land and sea to my own country, after you have afflicted me so greatly, let one of the people now waking speak a word of omen to me from within, and outside let some other portent from Zeus appear.”
sentences.n: This is a prayer. Zeus is addressed in the singular, but ἐθέλοντες, ἤγετ’ and ἐκακώσατε are plural, so he is speaking also to the other gods, through their father. τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν is 'the solid and the wet', that is land and sea. A φήμη is a spoken word that carries a meaning its speaker did not intend, a chance utterance taken as a sign. He asks for two signs: a φήμη from inside the house, and another portent from Zeus outside. φάσθω and φανήτω are third-person imperatives, 'let him say', 'let it appear'.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ euchomenos·
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying;
sentences.i: So he prayed;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is the formula that closes a speech, 'so he spoke'; ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο with its last vowel dropped before the next word. εὐχόμενος is the present participle of εὔχομαι, here 'praying'. The same verb can mean 'claim' when an infinitive follows it, as at line 192. The stop after it ends the prayer and hands over to the narrator.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε μητίετα Ζεύς,
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐβρόντησεν ἀπ’ αἰγλήεντος Ὀλύμπου,
ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ eklye mētieta Zeus,
autika d’ ebrontēsen ap’ aiglēentos Olympou,
hypsothen ek nepheōn·
sentences.i: and Zeus the counsellor heard him, and at once thundered from light-filled Olympus, from on high out of the clouds;
sentences.n: τοῦ is a genitive, 'him': κλύω 'hear' takes the genitive of the person heard. μητίετα is a nominative in -α, 'counsellor', from μῆτις 'counsel, plan'. αἰγλήεντος is built on αἴγλη 'gleam, radiance' with the suffix -ήεις 'full of', so 'full of light'. ἐβρόντησεν is the aorist of βροντάω 'thunder'. ὑψόθεν is 'from on high', with the suffix -θεν of direction from. ἐκ νεφέων is 'out of the clouds'; the woman says at line 114 that she sees no cloud.

sentences.t: γήθησε δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr: gēthēse de dios Odysseus.
sentences.l: and heavenly Odysseus rejoiced.
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus rejoiced.
sentences.n: γήθησε is the aorist of γηθέω 'rejoice', a poetic verb. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is 'heavenly Odysseus', δῖος being the stock epithet Homer gives him. His joy answers the thunder, the second of the signs he asked for in his prayer.

sentences.t:
φήμην δ’ ἐξ οἴκοιο γυνὴ προέηκεν ἀλετρὶς
πλησίον, ἔνθ’ ἄρα οἱ μύλαι ἥατο ποιμένι λαῶν,
τῇσιν δώδεκα πᾶσαι ἐπερρώοντο γυναῖκες
ἄλφιτα τεύχουσαι καὶ ἀλείατα, μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr:
phēmēn d’ ex oikoio gynē proeēken aletris
plēsion, enth’ ara hoi mylai hēato poimeni laōn,
tēisin dōdeka pasai eperrōonto gynaikes
alphita teuchousai kai aleiata, myelon andrōn.
sentences.l:
And a saying out of the house a woman sent forth, a grinding-woman,
near by, where for him the mills were set, for the shepherd of the people,
at which twelve, all of them, were busy, women,
making barley-meal and wheat-meal, the marrow of men.
sentences.i: Then a woman, a grinding-woman, sent out a word of omen from the house, close by, where the mills of the shepherd of the people stood. Twelve women in all were busy at them, making barley-meal and wheat-meal, the marrow of men.
sentences.n: φήμην is the word of the prayer taken up again: the first sign he asked for comes from inside the house, as he asked. ἀλετρίς is a woman who grinds grain, from ἀλέω 'grind', and μύλαι are hand-mills. ἥατο is the imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit', here 'were set, stood'. ποιμένι λαῶν 'shepherd of the people' is a title of a king, here of Odysseus, to whom the mills belong (οἱ 'for him'). τῇσιν is a dative plural, 'at which'. ἐπερρώοντο is from ἐπιρρώομαι 'move briskly, bestir oneself'. ἄλφιτα is barley-meal and ἀλείατα wheat-meal; calling them μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν 'marrow of men' makes meal what keeps men strong.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἄλλαι εὗδον, ἐπεὶ κατὰ πυρὸν ἄλεσσαν,
ἡ δὲ μί’ οὔπω παύετ’, ἀφαυροτάτη δ’ ἐτέτυκτο·
sentences.tr:
hai men ar’ allai heudon, epei kata pyron alessan,
hē de mi’ oupō pauet’, aphaurotatē d’ etetykto·
sentences.l:
The others, then, were asleep, since they had ground down their wheat,
but the one was not yet stopping, and she had been made the weakest;
sentences.i: The others were sleeping, for they had finished grinding their wheat, but one had not yet stopped, and she was the weakest of them;
sentences.n: εὗδον is the imperfect of εὕδω 'sleep', without augment. κατὰ … ἄλεσσαν is tmesis for κατήλεσαν, from ἀλέω 'grind'; ἄλεσσαν has the doubled σ of the older aorist, and πυρός is wheat. μί’ is μία 'one', elided. οὔπω παύετ’ is 'was not yet stopping', παύετο being the middle of παύω 'stop, cease'. ἀφαυροτάτη is the superlative of ἀφαυρός 'feeble'. ἐτέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω 'make', 'had been made', which stands for 'was'. She is the one left grinding.

sentences.t: ἥ ῥα μύλην στήσασα ἔπος φάτο, σῆμα ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr: hē rha mylēn stēsasa epos phato, sēma anakti·
sentences.l: She, having stopped the mill, spoke a word, a sign for the lord:
sentences.i: She stopped her mill and spoke a word, a sign for the lord:
sentences.n: ἥ ῥα is 'she, then'. στήσασα is the aorist participle of ἵστημι in its transitive sense, 'having made stand, stopped'. ἔπος φάτο 'spoke a word' is a stock phrase, φάτο being the unaugmented middle aorist of φημί. σῆμα ἄνακτι stands in apposition to ἔπος: the word is 'a sign for the lord', ἄνακτι being the dative of ἄναξ. The lord is the master of the mills, Odysseus. The raised dot points ahead to her words.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, ὅς τε θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ἀνάσσεις,
ἦ μεγάλ’ ἐβρόντησας ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος,
οὐδέ ποθι νέφος ἐστί·
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater, hos te theoisi kai anthrōpoisin anasseis,
ē megal’ ebrontēsas ap’ ouranou asteroentos,
oude pothi nephos esti·
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, you who rule over gods and men, you have thundered mightily from the starry sky, and there is no cloud anywhere;
sentences.n: Her prayer opens with the same words as Odysseus': Ζεῦ πάτερ. ὅς τε … ἀνάσσεις is 'you who rule', with ἀνάσσω taking the dative and the epic τε giving the statement the force of a standing fact; θεοῖσι and ἀνθρώποισιν are datives in -οισι(ν). ἦ μεγάλ’ is 'truly greatly', μεγάλα used as an adverb. ἐβρόντησας is the aorist of βροντάω. οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος is 'starry heaven'. οὐδέ ποθι νέφος ἐστί 'nor is there a cloud anywhere': she sees no cloud, which is why she takes the thunder for a portent.

sentences.t: τέρας νύ τεῳ τόδε φαίνεις.
sentences.tr: teras ny teōi tode phaineis.
sentences.l: a portent, now, to someone this you show.
sentences.i: this is a portent you are showing to someone.
sentences.n: τέρας is a portent, a sign sent by a god. τεῳ is the Ionic form of τινι, 'to someone'. νύ is a lighter form of νῦν, 'now, then'. τόδε is 'this' and φαίνεις 'you show'. She reasons that thunder out of a clear sky must be meant for somebody, but she does not guess for whom.

sentences.t: κρῆνον νῦν καὶ ἐμοὶ δειλῇ ἔπος, ὅττι κεν εἴπω·
sentences.tr: krēnon nyn kai emoi deilēi epos, hotti ken eipō·
sentences.l: Fulfil now also for me, miserable, the word, whatever I may say;
sentences.i: Fulfil now for me too, miserable as I am, the word I am about to say:
sentences.n: κρῆνον is the aorist imperative of κραίνω 'fulfil, bring to pass'; a god fulfils a word when what it says comes true. καὶ ἐμοὶ δειλῇ is 'for me too, miserable', δειλῇ being the feminine dative of δειλός, which means 'miserable, to be pitied', not 'cowardly'. ὅττι κεν εἴπω is 'whatever I shall say': ὅττι is ὅ τι, κεν is ἄν, and εἴπω is an aorist subjunctive.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες πύματόν τε καὶ ὕστατον ἤματι τῷδε
ἐν μεγάροις Ὀδυσῆος ἑλοίατο δαῖτ’ ἐρατεινήν,
sentences.tr:
mnēstēres pymaton te kai hystaton ēmati tōide
en megarois Odysēos heloiato dait’ erateinēn,
sentences.l:
May the suitors, for the last and final time on this day,
in the halls of Odysseus take their lovely feast,
sentences.i: May the suitors, on this very day, take their lovely feast in the halls of Odysseus for the last and final time,
sentences.n: This is a wish in the optative: ἑλοίατο is the aorist middle optative of αἱρέω 'take', with the ending -οίατο for -οιντο, 'may they take for themselves'. πύματον and ὕστατον both mean 'last', accusatives used as adverbs: 'for the last and final time'. ἤματι τῷδε is 'on this day', ἦμαρ being the epic word for ἡμέρα. Ὀδυσῆος has one σ where Ὀδυσσῆος has two. δαῖτ’ ἐρατεινήν is a 'lovely feast', and the adjective is bitter. The comma carries the sentence on to the relative clause.

sentences.t:
οἳ δή μοι καμάτῳ θυμαλγέι· γούνατ’ ἔλυσαν
ἄλφιτα τευχούσῃ·
sentences.tr:
hoi dē moi kamatōi thymalgei· gounat’ elysan
alphita teuchousēi·
sentences.l:
who indeed for me with heart-grieving toil have loosened my knees,
as I made barley-meal;
sentences.i: they who have loosened my knees with heart-grieving labour while I made barley-meal;
sentences.n: οἳ δή is 'who indeed'. καμάτῳ θυμαλγέι is a dative of cause, 'by heart-grieving toil'; θυμαλγής is built from θυμός 'heart' and ἄλγος 'pain'. γούνατ’ ἔλυσαν 'loosened my knees' means made me weak at the knees. τευχούσῃ is a feminine dative singular participle agreeing with μοι, 'to me as I made'. The text as printed has a raised dot after θυμαλγέι, in the middle of the clause; it marks no real pause, and the words read straight on.

sentences.t: νῦν ὕστατα δειπνήσειαν.
sentences.tr: nyn hystata deipnēseian.
sentences.l: now for the last time may they dine.”
sentences.i: May they dine now for the last time.”
sentences.n: νῦν ὕστατα is 'now for the last time', ὕστατα being a neuter plural used as an adverb. δειπνήσειαν is the aorist optative of δειπνέω 'dine', a wish again: 'may they dine'. The line sums up her prayer: she grinds the meal for the suitors' feast and asks that this be the last.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, χαῖρεν δὲ κλεηδόνι δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
Ζηνός τε βροντῇ·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, chairen de kleēdoni dios Odysseus
Zēnos te brontēi·
sentences.l:
So then she spoke, and rejoiced at the omen heavenly Odysseus
and at the thunder of Zeus;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and heavenly Odysseus rejoiced at the omen and at the thunder of Zeus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη 'so then she spoke' closes her speech; ἔφη is the augmented past of φημί. χαῖρεν is χαῖρε, the imperfect of χαίρω without augment, here with a dative 'at'. κλεηδών is a chance word heard as a sign, 'omen', from κλέος 'report'; it is the grinding-woman's φήμη. Ζηνός is the genitive of Ζεύς, and βροντῇ the dative of βροντή 'thunder'. Odysseus is glad at both signs, the word and the thunder.

sentences.t: φάτο γὰρ τίσασθαι ἀλείτας.
sentences.tr: phato gar tisasthai aleitas.
sentences.l: for he said he would take vengeance on the offenders.
sentences.i: for he said he would take vengeance on the offenders.
sentences.n: φάτο γάρ gives the reason for his joy: 'for he said'. φάτο is the unaugmented middle aorist of φημί. τίσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of τίνω; the middle means 'exact payment from, take vengeance on'. ἀλείτας is the accusative plural of ἀλείτης 'one who offends, a sinner'. When and to whom he said it is not stated here.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἄλλαι δμῳαὶ κατὰ δώματα κάλ’ Ὀδυσῆος
ἀγρόμεναι ἀνέκαιον ἐπ’ ἐσχάρῃ ἀκάματον πῦρ.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ allai dmōiai kata dōmata kal’ Odysēos
agromenai anekaion ep’ escharēi akamaton pyr.
sentences.l:
And the other maidservants through the fine halls of Odysseus,
having gathered, kindled on the hearth an untiring fire.
sentences.i: The other maids gathered throughout the fine halls of Odysseus and kindled an untiring fire on the hearth.
sentences.n: αἱ δ’ ἄλλαι is 'and the others', αἱ being the article-form used as a pronoun. δμῳαί are maidservants. κάλ’ is καλά 'fine' with the vowel elided. ἀγρόμεναι is the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω 'gather', with the short form ἀγρόμενος for ἀγερόμενος. ἀνέκαιον is the imperfect of ἀνακαίω 'kindle'. ἐσχάρη is a hearth. ἀκάματον 'untiring' is ἀ- 'not' with κάματος 'toil, weariness': a fire that does not tire, that is one that keeps burning.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ εὐνῆθεν ἀνίστατο, ἰσόθεος φώς,
εἵματα ἑσσάμενος·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos d’ eunēthen anistato, isotheos phōs,
heimata hessamenos·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus from his bed rose up, a man equal to a god,
his clothes having put on;
sentences.i: Telemachus, a man the equal of a god, rose from his bed and put on his clothes;
sentences.n: The scene turns from Odysseus to his son. εὐνῆθεν is 'from his bed', εὐνή with the suffix -θεν of direction from. ἀνίστατο is the imperfect middle of ἀνίστημι, 'was rising'. ἰσόθεος φώς is 'a man equal to a god', ἰσόθεος 'equal to a god' and φώς a poetic word for 'man'. εἵματα ἑσσάμενος is 'having put on clothes', ἑσσάμενος being the aorist middle participle of ἕννυμι 'clothe'. The unit ends in the middle of line 125, at the stop after the participle.

sentences.t: περὶ δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ θέτ’ ὤμῳ·
sentences.tr: peri de xiphos oxy thet’ ōmōi·
sentences.l: and round, a sharp sword he set on his shoulder;
sentences.i: and slung a sharp sword about his shoulder;
sentences.n: περὶ δὲ … θέτ’ is tmesis: the preverb περί stands apart from its verb, which together are 'put around'. θέτ’ is θέτο, the aorist middle of τίθημι without augment, 'put for himself'. ξίφος ὀξύ is 'a sharp sword', and ὤμῳ the dative of ὦμος 'shoulder'. The unit begins in the middle of line 125.

sentences.t:
ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος, ἀκαχμένον ὀξέι· χαλκῷ·
sentences.tr:
possi d’ hypo liparoisin edēsato kala pedila,
heileto d’ alkimon enchos, akachmenon oxei· chalkōi·
sentences.l:
and under his sleek feet he bound fine sandals,
and took up his sturdy spear, tipped with sharp bronze;
sentences.i: he bound fine sandals beneath his sleek feet, and took up his sturdy spear, tipped with sharp bronze;
sentences.n: ποσσί is the dative plural of πούς 'foot' in its older form. ὑπὸ … ἐδήσατο is tmesis for 'bound beneath', the aorist middle of δέω 'bind'. λιπαροῖσιν 'sleek' describes the feet, and πέδιλα are sandals. εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω 'take'. ἀκαχμένον is a perfect passive participle from the root ἀκ- 'point', 'tipped, pointed', with the dative ὀξέι χαλκῷ 'with sharp bronze'. The text as printed has a raised dot after ὀξέι, in the middle of the phrase; it marks no real pause, and ὀξέι χαλκῷ read together.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών, πρὸς δ’ Εὐρύκλειαν ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: stē d’ ar’ ep’ oudon iōn, pros d’ Eurykleian eeipe·
sentences.l: and he stood on the threshold, going, and to Eurycleia he said:
sentences.i: and he went and stood on the threshold, and said to Eurycleia:
sentences.n: στῆ is ἔστη, the aorist of ἵστημι, without augment. ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών is 'having gone to the threshold': οὐδός is the threshold and ἰών the participle of εἶμι 'go'. πρὸς … ἔειπε is tmesis for 'spoke to', ἔειπε being the aorist εἶπε with the older double vowel. The raised dot introduces his words.

sentences.t:
μαῖα φίλη, τὸν ξεῖνον ἐτιμήσασθ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
εὐνῇ καὶ σίτῳ, ἦ αὔτως κεῖται ἀκηδής;
sentences.tr:
maia philē, ton xeinon etimēsasth’ eni oikōi
eunēi kai sitōi, ē autōs keitai akēdēs;
sentences.l:
“Dear nurse, have you honoured the stranger in the house
with bed and food, or does he lie just so, uncared for?
sentences.i: “Dear nurse, have you honoured the stranger in the house with a bed and with food, or does he lie there just as he is, uncared for?
sentences.n: μαῖα is a respectful address to an older woman, here the nurse; φίλη is 'dear'. ἐτιμήσασθ’ is ἐτιμήσασθε, second person plural of the aorist middle of τιμάω 'honour'; the address μαῖα is singular, and the line does not say whom the plural includes, perhaps the women of the household under her. εὐνῇ καὶ σίτῳ are datives of means, 'with bed and food'. ἦ is 'or', opening the second half of the question. αὔτως is 'just so, as he is'. κεῖται is 'lies'. ἀκηδής is 'uncared for' (it can also mean 'careless'). Line 130 is regular only with licences: hiatus is left open after σίτῳ and before αὔτως, and κεῖται is shortened before ἀκηδής; it has just one dactyl, so it reads heavily.

sentences.t: τοιαύτη γὰρ ἐμὴ μήτηρ, πινυτή περ ἐοῦσα·
sentences.tr: toiautē gar emē mētēr, pinytē per eousa·
sentences.l: for such is my mother, discerning though she is;
sentences.i: for my mother is such a one, discerning though she is;
sentences.n: τοιαύτη is 'of such a kind', and it sets up the description that follows. ἐμὴ μήτηρ is 'my mother', Telemachus speaking of Penelope without naming her. πινυτή is 'discerning'. περ with the participle ἐοῦσα (= οὖσα) is concessive: 'although she is'.

sentences.t:
ἐμπλήγδην ἕτερόν γε τίει μερόπων ἀνθρώπων
χείρονα, τὸν δέ τ’ ἀρείον’ ἀτιμήσασ’ ἀποπέμπει.
sentences.tr:
emplēgdēn heteron ge tiei meropōn anthrōpōn
cheirona, ton de t’ areion’ atimēsas’ apopempei.
sentences.l:
at random another of speech-dividing men she honours,
a worse one, and the better, having dishonoured, she sends away.”
sentences.i: she honours at random some man of articulate speech who is worse, and sends away the better one after dishonouring him.”
sentences.n: ἐμπλήγδην is 'at random', related to ἐμπλήσσω 'strike upon'. ἕτερον is 'another, some other man', and it is set against τὸν … ἀρείον’, 'the better', where ἀρείον’ is ἀρείονα, the comparative of ἀγαθός. χείρονα is 'worse'. τίει is the present of τίω 'honour'; ἀτιμήσασ’ is the aorist participle of ἀτιμάω 'dishonour'; ἀποπέμπει is 'sends away'. μερόπων ἀνθρώπων: the meaning of μέροπες is not known; the old explanation 'having divided speech', that is articulate, is followed, and 'mortal' is the other guess. τε in τὸν δέ τ’ marks a general statement.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν is the pronoun 'him'. αὖτε is 'in turn, again', and it marks a reply. προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον 'speak to, address'. περίφρων 'circumspect' is the stock epithet of the nurse here, built from περί and φρήν 'mind'. The nurse answers the young man's complaint about his mother.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἄν μιν νῦν, τέκνον, ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳο.
sentences.tr: ouk an min nyn, teknon, anaition aitioōio.
sentences.l: “Not him now, child, blameless, would you blame.
sentences.i: “You should not blame him now, my child, when he is blameless.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἄν … αἰτιόῳο is an optative with ἄν, 'you would not blame', used as gentle advice, 'you should not'. αἰτιόῳο is the second singular optative of αἰτιάομαι 'blame', in the Homeric form with the vowels spread apart (diectasis), where Attic has αἰτιῷο. μιν is 'him'. ἀναίτιον is 'blameless', a predicate: 'when he is not to blame'. τέκνον 'child' is how an old nurse speaks to a young man. νῦν is 'now'.

sentences.t:
οἶνον μὲν γὰρ πῖνε καθήμενος, ὄφρ’ ἔθελ’ αὐτός,
σίτου δ’ οὐκέτ’ ἔφη πεινήμεναι·
sentences.tr:
oinon men gar pine kathēmenos, ophr’ ethel’ autos,
sitou d’ ouket’ ephē peinēmenai·
sentences.l:
For wine he drank, sitting, as long as he himself wished,
but of food he said he was no longer hungry;
sentences.i: He sat and drank wine for as long as he wished, but of food he said he was hungry no longer;
sentences.n: μὲν γάρ … σίτου δέ sets 'wine' against 'food'. πῖνε is the imperfect of πίνω without augment. καθήμενος is 'sitting'. ὄφρ’ ἔθελ’ αὐτός is 'as long as he himself wished', ὄφρα being 'as long as' and ἔθελ’ ἔθελε, without augment. οὐκέτ’ ἔφη πεινήμεναι is 'he no longer said he was hungry', πεινήμεναι being the infinitive of πεινάω in -μεναι, and σίτου the genitive 'for food'.

sentences.t: εἴρετο γάρ μιν.
sentences.tr: eireto gar min.
sentences.l: for she asked him.
sentences.i: for she asked him.
sentences.n: εἴρετο is the imperfect middle of εἴρομαι 'ask' (Attic ἤρετο), and μιν is 'him'. No subject is named, and this part does not say who asked; the 'she' of ἡ μέν in line 139 may be the same person, perhaps the mistress of the house, but that is a guess. γάρ gives the reason for what precedes: he said he was hungry no longer, for he had been asked.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ κοίτοιο καὶ ὕπνου μιμνήσκοιτο,
ἡ μὲν δέμνι’ ἄνωγεν ὑποστορέσαι δμῳῇσιν,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē koitoio kai hypnou mimnēskoito,
hē men demni’ anōgen hypostoresai dmōiēisin,
sentences.l:
But when he thought of bed and sleep,
she indeed bade the maidservants spread bedding under him,
sentences.i: But when he came to think of bed and sleep, she told her maids to spread bedding for him,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή is 'but when at length'. μιμνήσκοιτο is an optative, 'he came to think of', and μιμνήσκομαι takes the genitive κοίτοιο καὶ ὕπνου 'of bed and of sleep'. ἡ μέν is 'she, for her part', the article-form as a pronoun, set against αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ in the next unit. ἄνωγεν is 'bade', from ἄνωγα, a perfect used as a present with a past form. ὑποστορέσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὑποστόρνυμι 'spread beneath'. δμῳῇσιν is the dative plural of δμῳή, 'to the maids'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’, ὥς τις πάμπαν ὀϊζυρὸς καὶ ἄποτμος,
οὐκ ἔθελ’ ἐν λέκτροισι καὶ ἐν ῥήγεσσι καθεύδειν,
ἀλλ’ ἐν ἀδεψήτῳ βοέῃ καὶ κώεσιν οἰῶν
ἔδραθ’ ἐνὶ προδόμῳ·
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’, hōs tis pampan oïzyros kai apotmos,
ouk ethel’ en lektroisi kai en rhēgessi katheudein,
all’ en adepsētōi boeēi kai kōesin oiōn
edrath’ eni prodomōi·
sentences.l:
but he, like a man utterly sorrowful and ill-fated,
was not willing in a bed and on rugs to sleep,
but on an untanned oxhide and the fleeces of sheep
he slept in the fore-house;
sentences.i: but he, like a man wholly sorrowful and ill-fated, would not sleep in a bed or on rugs, and slept on an untanned oxhide and sheep’s fleeces in the vestibule;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ is 'but he', the pronoun-article again. ὥς τις is 'like some', with accented ὥς 'as'. ὀϊζυρός 'sorrowful' and ἄποτμος 'ill-fated', from ἀ- and πότμος 'lot, fate', are joined by καί, with πάμπαν 'altogether'. ῥήγεσσι is the dative plural of ῥῆγος 'rug'. ἀδεψήτῳ βοέῃ is 'untanned oxhide', the dative of βοέη, and κώεσιν οἰῶν is 'fleeces of sheep', οἰῶν being the genitive plural of οἶς. ἔδραθ’ is ἔδραθε, the aorist of δαρθάνω 'sleep'. The προδόμος is the space in front of the hall, the fore-house.

sentences.t: χλαῖναν δ’ ἐπιέσσαμεν ἡμεῖς.
sentences.tr: chlainan d’ epiessamen hēmeis.
sentences.l: and a cloak we put over him, we ourselves.”
sentences.i: and we ourselves covered him with a cloak.”
sentences.n: χλαῖναν is a cloak, the accusative object. ἐπιέσσαμεν is the aorist of ἐπιέννυμι 'put on as a covering', first person plural: Eurycleia includes herself and the household. ἡμεῖς is emphatic, 'we ourselves did it'. The stop closes her speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
ἔγχος ἔχων, ἅμα τῷ γε δύω κύνες ἀργοὶ ἕποντο.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Tēlemachos de diek megaroio bebēkei
enchos echōn, hama tōi ge dyō kynes argoi heponto.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and Telemachus through the hall had gone,
holding his spear; along with him two swift dogs followed.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Telemachus went out through the hall, holding his spear, and two swift dogs followed along with him.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is 'so she spoke', the speaker here being the nurse. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, 'had gone', which English renders as 'went'. διὲκ μεγάροιο is 'out through the hall', with a genitive in -οιο. ἔγχος ἔχων is 'holding his spear'. ἅμα τῷ γε is 'along with him', τῷ being a pronoun. δύω is 'two'. κύνες ἀργοί: ἀργός means 'swift' or 'white', and the ancient commentators disagreed; 'swift' is kept. ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow', without augment.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν εἰς ἀγορὴν μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr: bē d’ imen eis agorēn met’ eÿknēmidas Achaious.
sentences.l: And he set out to go to the assembly among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: He set out for the place of assembly, to join the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω without augment, and ἴμεν the old infinitive of εἶμι 'go': βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is 'he set out to go'. ἀγορή is both an assembly and the place where it meets. μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς is μετά with the accusative, 'among', ἐϋκνήμιδες being 'well-greaved', from εὖ and κνημίς 'greave'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αὖτε δμῳῇσιν ἐκέκλετο δῖα γυναικῶν,
Εὐρύκλει’, Ὦπος θυγάτηρ Πεισηνορίδαο·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ aute dmōiēisin ekekleto dia gynaikōn,
Euryklei’, Ōpos thygatēr Peisēnoridao·
sentences.l:
And she in turn to the maidservants called out, heavenly-one of women,
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor:
sentences.i: And she in turn gave orders to the maids, heavenly among women, Eurycleia, daughter of Ops son of Peisenor:
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ αὖτε is 'and she in turn'. ἐκέκλετο is the reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι 'call out to, give orders to', and it takes the dative δμῳῇσιν. δῖα γυναικῶν is 'heavenly among women', δῖα being the feminine of δῖος and γυναικῶν a partitive genitive; it is said here of Eurycleia. Ὦπος is the genitive of Ops, and Πεισηνορίδαο is a patronymic, the genitive of Πεισηνορίδης 'son of Peisenor', and it agrees with Ὦπος: she is the daughter of Ops, and Ops is Peisenor’s son, so Peisenor is her grandfather. The raised dot introduces her orders.

sentences.t:
ἀγρεῖθ’, αἱ μὲν δῶμα κορήσατε ποιπνύσασαι,
ῥάσσατέ τ’, ἔν τε θρόνοις εὐποιήτοισι τάπητας
βάλλετε πορφυρέους·
sentences.tr:
agreith’, hai men dōma korēsate poipnysasai,
rhassate t’, en te thronois eupoiētoisi tapētas
ballete porphyreous·
sentences.i: “Come, some of you sweep the house, bustling about, and sprinkle it, and throw purple carpets on the well-made chairs;
sentences.n: ἀγρεῖθ’ is ἀγρεῖτε, the plural of ἄγρει, an exclamation 'come on' related to ἀγρέω 'seize'; τ turns to θ before the rough breathing of the next word. αἱ μέν … αἱ δέ … ταὶ δέ split the maids into groups, the article-forms again pronouns: 'some … others … others'. κορήσατε is the aorist imperative of κορέω 'sweep', and ποιπνύσασαι the aorist participle of ποιπνύω 'bustle'. ῥάσσατε is the aorist imperative of ῥαίνω 'sprinkle'; no object is stated, and the house is understood. θρόνοις εὐποιήτοισι are 'well-made chairs', τάπητας 'carpets', πορφυρέους 'purple'.

sentences.t:
αἱ δὲ σπόγγοισι τραπέζας
πάσας ἀμφιμάσασθε, καθήρατε δὲ κρητῆρας
καὶ δέπα ἀμφικύπελλα τετυγμένα·
sentences.tr:
hai de spongoisi trapezas
pasas amphimasasthe, kathērate de krētēras
kai depa amphikypella tetygmena·
sentences.i: others wipe all the tables over with sponges, and clean the mixing-bowls and the well-wrought double cups;
sentences.n: σπόγγοισι is a dative of means, 'with sponges'. ἀμφιμάσασθε is the aorist middle imperative of ἀμφιμάομαι 'wipe all round', with πάσας 'all' agreeing with τραπέζας. καθήρατε is the aorist imperative of καθαίρω 'clean'. κρητῆρες are the large bowls in which wine and water were mixed. δέπα ἀμφικύπελλα are 'double cups', δέπα being the plural of δέπας; whether ἀμφικύπελλον means 'double' or 'two-handled' is disputed. τετυγμένα 'well-wrought' is the perfect passive participle of τεύχω.

sentences.t:
ταὶ δὲ μεθ’ ὕδωρ
ἔρχεσθε κρήνηνδε, καὶ οἴσετε θᾶσσον ἰοῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
tai de meth’ hydōr
erchesthe krēnēnde, kai oisete thasson iousai.
sentences.l:
and you others, for water
go to the spring, and bring it quickly, going.
sentences.i: and the rest of you, go to the spring for water and bring it quickly.
sentences.n: ταὶ δέ is 'and the others': ταί is the feminine nominative plural article-form used as a pronoun. μεθ’ ὕδωρ is μετά with the accusative, 'after water', that is 'to fetch water'. κρήνηνδε is 'to the spring', with the suffix -δε of direction. ἔρχεσθε is the present imperative; οἴσετε, from the stem of the future οἴσω, is also an imperative, 'bring'. θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, 'faster', which in a command means 'quickly, at once'. ἰοῦσαι is the feminine participle of εἶμι, 'going'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ δὴν μνηστῆρες ἀπέσσονται μεγάροιο,
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἦρι νέονται, ἐπεὶ καὶ πᾶσιν ἑορτή.
sentences.tr:
ou gar dēn mnēstēres apessontai megaroio,
alla mal’ ēri neontai, epei kai pasin heortē.
sentences.l:
for not for long will the suitors be away from the hall,
but very early they will come back, since for all there is a festival.”
sentences.i: For the suitors will not be away from the hall for long; they will come back very early, since it is a festival for everyone.”
sentences.n: δήν is 'for long', and οὐ γὰρ δήν 'for not for long'. ἀπέσσονται, from ἄπειμι 'be away', is a future with the doubled σ of the older form, and μεγάροιο is a genitive 'from the hall'. ἦρι is 'early'. νέονται is a present of νέομαι 'go back, return' with future sense. ἐπεὶ καὶ πᾶσιν ἑορτή is 'since there is a festival for everyone too', with ἐστί understood. This line gives the reason for the haste; the festival is not named in it.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἱ δ’ ἄρα τῆς μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hai d’ ara tēs mala men klyon ēd’ epithonto.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and they then readily heard her and obeyed.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and they listened to her readily and obeyed.
sentences.n: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of αἱ. αἱ δ’ ἄρα is 'and they then', αἱ the article-form as pronoun. κλύον is the unaugmented ἔκλυον, a past tense of κλύω 'hear', which takes the genitive τῆς 'her'. ἐπίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθω, 'obeyed'. μάλα μὲν … ἠδ’ is 'readily … and', ἠδέ being a poetic 'and'.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἐείκοσι βῆσαν ἐπὶ κρήνην μελάνυδρον,
αἱ δ’ αὐτοῦ κατὰ δώματ’ ἐπισταμένως πονέοντο.
sentences.tr:
hai men eeikosi bēsan epi krēnēn melanydron,
hai d’ autou kata dōmat’ epistamenōs poneonto.
sentences.l:
Twenty of them went to the dark-watered spring,
and the others there throughout the halls skilfully toiled.
sentences.i: Twenty of them went to the dark-watered spring, while the others set to work there in the halls with skill.
sentences.n: αἱ μὲν ἐείκοσι is 'twenty of them', ἐείκοσι being the epic form of εἴκοσι. βῆσαν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, third plural. κρήνην μελάνυδρον is a 'dark-watered spring', μελάνυδρος being built from μέλας 'dark, black' and ὕδωρ 'water'. αὐτοῦ is 'there, on the spot'. ἐπισταμένως 'skilfully' comes from ἐπίσταμαι 'know how'. πονέοντο is the uncontracted form of πονοῦντο, the imperfect middle of πονέομαι 'toil'.

sentences.t: ἐς δ’ ἦλθον δρηστῆρες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: es d’ ēlthon drēstēres Achaiōn.
sentences.l: And in came the serving-men of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Then the serving-men of the Achaeans came in.
sentences.n: ἐς … ἦλθον is tmesis for 'came in'. δρηστῆρες are serving-men, from δράω 'do, serve'. Ἀχαιῶν 'of the Achaeans' is the poem's general name for the Greeks; which Achaeans these men serve is not said in this line. The full stop closes the sentence in the middle of line 160.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα
εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως κέασαν ξύλα, ταὶ δὲ γυναῖκες
ἦλθον ἀπὸ κρήνης·
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeita
eu kai epistamenōs keasan xyla, tai de gynaikes
ēlthon apo krēnēs·
sentences.i: They split the wood well and skilfully, and the women came back from the spring;
sentences.n: οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα … ταὶ δὲ γυναῖκες is 'they then … but the women', the article-forms again pronouns. κέασαν is the unaugmented aorist of κεάζω 'split', and ξύλα are logs or firewood. εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως is 'well and skilfully'. ἦλθον ἀπὸ κρήνης is 'came from the spring'. The unit begins in the middle of line 160.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δέ σφισιν ἦλθε συβώτης
τρεῖς σιάλους κατάγων, οἳ ἔσαν μετὰ πᾶσιν ἄριστοι.
sentences.tr:
epi de sphisin ēlthe sybōtēs
treis sialous katagōn, hoi esan meta pasin aristoi.
sentences.l:
and upon them came the swineherd,
bringing three fat hogs, which were among all the best.
sentences.i: and after them came the swineherd, bringing three fat hogs, the best among them all.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ δέ σφισιν ἦλθε is 'and after them came', ἐπί being an adverb and σφισιν the dative 'them'. συβώτης is a swineherd; he is not named in this line. σίαλος is a fattened hog, and κατάγων is 'bringing down'. οἳ ἔσαν μετὰ πᾶσιν ἄριστοι is 'which were best among all', ἔσαν being ἦσαν and ἄριστοι 'best'.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοὺς μέν ῥ’ εἴασε καθ’ ἕρκεα καλὰ νέμεσθαι,
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ Ὀδυσῆα προσηύδα μειλιχίοισι·
sentences.tr:
kai tous men rh’ eiase kath’ herkea kala nemesthai,
autos d’ aut’ Odysēa prosēuda meilichioisi·
sentences.l:
And those indeed he let graze about the fine enclosures,
and he himself in turn spoke to Odysseus with gentle ones:
sentences.i: He let the hogs graze about the fine enclosures, and he himself in turn spoke to Odysseus with gentle words:
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν is 'those', the hogs, set against αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’, 'and he himself in turn'. ῥ’ is ῥα. εἴασε is the aorist of ἐάω 'allow', and νέμεσθαι the middle infinitive of νέμω, 'to graze'. ἕρκεα is the plural of ἕρκος 'fence, enclosure', and καλά is 'fine'. προσηύδα takes the accusative Ὀδυσῆα. μειλιχίοισι is an adjective in the dative plural, 'with gentle ones', the noun 'words' being understood.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἦ ἄρ τί σε μᾶλλον Ἀχαιοὶ εἰσορόωσιν,
ἦέ σ’ ἀτιμάζουσι κατὰ μέγαρ’, ὡς τὸ πάρος περ;
sentences.tr:
xein’, ē ar ti se mallon Achaioi eisoroōsin,
ēe s’ atimazousi kata megar’, hōs to paros per;
sentences.l:
“Stranger, do the Achaeans then at all more regard you,
or do they dishonour you in the halls, as before?”
sentences.i: “Stranger, do the Achaeans show you any more regard now, or do they dishonour you in the halls, as before?”
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε, the vocative of ξεῖνος 'stranger'. The question has two halves, ἦ ἄρ … ἦέ, 'is it then that … or'. μᾶλλον is 'more'. εἰσορόωσιν is the uncontracted form of εἰσορῶσιν, 'look upon, regard'. ἀτιμάζουσι is 'dishonour', from ἀ- and τιμή 'honour'. κατὰ μέγαρ’ is κατὰ μέγαρα, 'through the hall'. ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is 'just as before'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολυμήτις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: This is the reply-formula τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη, 'answering him, addressed'. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι 'reply', and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to'. πολυμήτις Ὀδυσσεύς: πολύμητις is 'of many wiles', from πολύς and μῆτις 'cunning intelligence'; this line prints the accent πολυμήτις where line 183 has πολύμητις, it is the same word with a different accent mark, and the line scans as an ordinary hexameter.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ δή, Εὔμαιε, θεοὶ τισαίατο λώβην,
ἣν οἵδ’ ὑβρίζοντες ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωνται
οἴκῳ ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ, οὐδ’ αἰδοῦς μοῖραν ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr:
ai gar dē, Eumaie, theoi tisaiato lōbēn,
hēn hoid’ hybrizontes atasthala mēchanoōntai
oikōi en allotriōi, oud’ aidous moiran echousin.
sentences.l:
“Would that indeed, Eumaeus, the gods would take vengeance for the outrage
which these, being insolent, devise as wanton deeds
in another’s house, and they have no share of shame.”
sentences.i: “If only the gods would take vengeance, Eumaeus, for the outrage that these men in their insolence devise as wanton deeds in another man’s house, and they have no share of shame.”
sentences.n: αἲ γὰρ δή 'would that indeed' opens a wish, with the optative τισαίατο, the aorist middle of τίνω with the ending -αίατο for -αιντο: 'may they take vengeance for'. λώβη is 'outrage, insult'. Εὔμαιε is the vocative, naming the swineherd. ἣν οἵδ’: ἥν is the relative, 'which', and οἵδε 'these men here'. ὑβρίζοντες is 'acting insolently'. ἀτάσθαλα 'wanton things' is a neuter plural, which can be read as what they devise or as 'wantonly'. μηχανόωνται is uncontracted μηχανῶνται. οὐδ’ αἰδοῦς μοῖραν ἔχουσιν is 'nor have they a share of αἰδώς', the shame that holds a man back from what is improper.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
ἀγχίμολον δέ σφ’ ἦλθε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
anchimolon de sph’ ēlthe Melanthios, aipolos aigōn.
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
and close by them came Melanthius, the goatherd of goats.
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, and Melanthius the goatherd of the goats came up close to them.
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μέν is 'so they, for their part'. τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον is 'such things to one another they were saying', ἀγόρευον being the imperfect of ἀγορεύω 'speak'. ἀγχίμολον is an adverb, 'close by', and σφ’ is 'them', elided. Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν is 'Melanthius, goatherd of goats': an αἰπόλος is a goatherd, and αἰγῶν names the animals again. A new arrival begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t:
αἶγας ἄγων αἳ πᾶσι μετέπρεπον αἰπολίοισι,
δεῖπνον μνηστήρεσσι.
sentences.tr:
aigas agōn hai pasi meteprepon aipolioisi,
deipnon mnēstēressi.
sentences.l:
goats driving, which among all the herds of goats were outstanding,
as a meal for the suitors.
sentences.i: He was driving goats that were outstanding among all the herds of goats, to be a meal for the suitors.
sentences.n: αἶγας ἄγων is 'driving goats', ἄγων being the participle of ἄγω. αἳ πᾶσι μετέπρεπον αἰπολίοισι is 'which stood out among all the herds of goats': μετέπρεπον is the imperfect of μεταπρέπω 'be conspicuous among', and αἰπολίοισι the dative plural of αἰπόλιον 'herd of goats'. δεῖπνον μνηστήρεσσι is 'a meal for the suitors', with μνηστήρεσσι a dative in -εσσι.

sentences.t: δύω δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο νομῆες.
sentences.tr: dyō d’ ham’ heponto nomēes.
sentences.l: and two herdsmen followed along with him.
sentences.i: Two herdsmen followed along with him.
sentences.n: δύω is 'two', and νομῆες 'herdsmen', from νέμω 'tend, graze'. ἅμ’ is ἅμα 'along with', and ἕποντο the imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow', without augment. The herdsmen are not named here.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰς μὲν κατέδησεν ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ,
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ Ὀδυσῆα προσηύδα κερτομίοισι·
sentences.tr:
kai tas men katedēsen hyp’ aithousēi eridoupōi,
autos d’ aut’ Odysēa prosēuda kertomioisi·
sentences.l:
And them indeed he tied up beneath the loud-echoing portico,
and he himself in turn spoke to Odysseus with taunting ones:
sentences.i: He tied the goats up under the loud-echoing portico, and he himself in turn spoke to Odysseus with taunts:
sentences.n: Like line 164, this unit sets the animals against the man: καὶ τὰς μέν … αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’. τάς is the feminine 'them', the goats. κατέδησεν is the aorist of καταδέω 'tie up'. ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ is 'under the loud-echoing portico': αἴθουσα is the roofed portico of the house, and ἐρίδουπος 'loud-sounding' is built from ἐρι- (an intensive) and δοῦπος 'a heavy sound'. κερτομίοισι is a dative plural adjective, 'taunting', used for 'words' as μειλιχίοισι was: κερτόμιος means 'cutting, taunting'.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐνθάδ’ ἀνιήσεις κατὰ δῶμα
ἀνέρας αἰτίζων, ἀτὰρ οὐκ ἔξεισθα θύραζε;
sentences.tr:
xein’, eti kai nyn enthad’ aniēseis kata dōma
aneras aitizōn, atar ouk exeistha thyraze;
sentences.l:
“Stranger, still even now here will you distress throughout the house
men, begging, and will you not go out of doors?
sentences.i: “Stranger, will you go on causing distress here even now, throughout the house, begging from the men, and will you still not go out of doors?
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is the address Eumaeus used to Odysseus, now said with contempt. ἔτι καὶ νῦν is 'still even now'. ἀνιήσεις is the future of ἀνιάω 'distress, be a trouble to'; its object is ἀνέρας 'men' (Attic ἄνδρας), and αἰτίζων 'begging' qualifies the subject. ἀτάρ is 'but, and yet'. οὐκ ἔξεισθα θύραζε is a question: ἔξεισθα is the second singular of ἔξειμι 'go out', in the old ending -σθα, with a future sense, and θύραζε 'out of doors' has the suffix -ζε of direction.

sentences.t:
πάντως οὐκέτι νῶϊ διακρινέεσθαι ὀΐω
πρὶν χειρῶν γεύσασθαι, ἐπεὶ σύ περ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον
αἰτίζεις·
sentences.tr:
pantōs ouketi nōï diakrineesthai oïō
prin cheirōn geusasthai, epei sy per ou kata kosmon
aitizeis·
sentences.i: I think, at any rate, that the two of us will not be parted any more before we have had a taste of each other’s hands, for you do not beg in due order;
sentences.n: πάντως is 'altogether, in any case'. νῶϊ is the dual 'we two', and διακρινέεσθαι the future passive infinitive of διακρίνω 'separate', which depends on ὀΐω 'I think': 'that we two will be separated'. πρὶν … γεύσασθαι is 'before tasting', the aorist infinitive of γεύομαι with the genitive χειρῶν 'of hands'; to have a taste of hands is to come to blows. κατὰ κόσμον is 'in due order, as is fitting'. σύ περ is 'you for your part'.

sentences.t: εἰσὶν δὲ καὶ ἄλλαι δαῖτες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: eisin de kai allai daites Achaiōn.
sentences.l: and there are other feasts of the Achaeans too.”
sentences.i: and there are other feasts of the Achaeans as well.”
sentences.n: εἰσὶν δὲ καὶ ἄλλαι δαῖτες Ἀχαιῶν is 'and there are other feasts of the Achaeans too'. δαῖτες is the plural of δαίς 'feast'. The sense is that Odysseus should beg elsewhere. The stop ends Melanthius' speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἀλλ’ ἀκέων κίνησε κάρη, κακὰ βυσσοδομεύων.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, ton d’ ou ti prosephē polymētis Odysseus,
all’ akeōn kinēse karē, kaka byssodomeuōn.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, but him not at all did many-wiled Odysseus address,
but in silence he shook his head, evils devising deep within.
sentences.i: So he spoke, but Odysseus of many wiles gave him no word at all in reply, but in silence he shook his head, devising evil deep within.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is 'so he spoke'. τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη is 'and him not at all did he address'. πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς is 'Odysseus of many wiles'. ἀκέων is 'in silence', and κίνησε κάρη 'he shook his head', κάρη being an old neuter noun for 'head' and κίνησε an aorist without augment. κακὰ βυσσοδομεύων is 'devising evil deep within', the verb built from βυσσός 'depth' and a stem meaning 'build, contrive'. He swallows the insult and says nothing.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπὶ τρίτος ἦλθε Φιλοίτιος, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν,
βοῦν στεῖραν μνηστῆρσιν ἄγων καὶ πίονας αἶγας.
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ epi tritos ēlthe Philoitios, orchamos andrōn,
boun steiran mnēstērsin agōn kai pionas aigas.
sentences.l:
And after them as third came Philoetius, chief of men,
bringing a barren cow for the suitors and fat goats.
sentences.i: Third after them came Philoetius, chief of men, bringing a barren cow and fat goats for the suitors.
sentences.n: τοῖσι δ’ ἐπί is 'and after them', ἐπί being an adverb. τρίτος is 'third', the third of the newcomers. Φιλοίτιος is Philoetius, and ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν 'chief of men' is the title given with his name. βοῦν στεῖραν is a barren cow, and μνηστῆρσιν the contracted dative of μνηστήρ. πίονας αἶγας are 'fat goats'.

sentences.t:
πορθμῆες δ’ ἄρα τούς γε διήγαγον, οἵ τε καὶ ἄλλους
ἀνθρώπους πέμπουσιν, ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκηται.
sentences.tr:
porthmēes d’ ara tous ge diēgagon, hoi te kai allous
anthrōpous pempousin, hotis spheas eisaphikētai.
sentences.l:
And ferrymen then had brought these across, who also other
men convey, whoever to them comes.
sentences.i: Ferrymen had brought them across, those who convey other men too, whoever comes to them.
sentences.n: πορθμῆες are ferrymen, from πόρος 'crossing'. τούς γε is 'them', a masculine plural that the line does not explain (Philoetius and whatever or whoever came with him), and διήγαγον the aorist of διάγω 'bring across'. οἵ τε καὶ ἄλλους is 'who also others', with epic τε giving a general description of what ferrymen do. ὅτις is the Homeric form of ὅστις, 'whoever', and σφέας is 'them'. εἰσαφίκηται is the aorist subjunctive of εἰσαφικνέομαι 'arrive at', singular after ὅτις. The line does not say what water they crossed.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν εὖ κατέδησεν ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ,
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ ἐρέεινε συβώτην ἄγχι παραστάς·
sentences.tr:
kai ta men eu katedēsen hyp’ aithousēi eridoupōi,
autos d’ aut’ ereeine sybōtēn anchi parastas·
sentences.l:
And these indeed he tied up well beneath the loud-echoing portico,
and he himself in turn questioned the swineherd, standing close by:
sentences.i: He tied up the animals securely under the loud-echoing portico, and he himself in turn questioned the swineherd, standing close beside him:
sentences.n: καὶ τὰ μὲν εὖ κατέδησεν: τά is the neuter plural 'those', the cow and the goats, and εὖ is 'well, securely'. ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ is the same place as at line 176. αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ ἐρέεινε συβώτην is 'and he himself in turn questioned the swineherd': ἐρέεινε is the imperfect of ἐρεείνω 'ask, question'. ἄγχι παραστάς is 'standing close by', παραστάς being the aorist participle of παρίστημι.

sentences.t:
τίς δὴ ὅδε ξεῖνος νέον εἰλήλουθε, συβῶτα,
ἡμέτερον πρὸς δῶμα;
sentences.tr:
tis dē hode xeinos neon eilēlouthe, sybōta,
hēmeteron pros dōma;
sentences.l:
“Who, then, is this stranger, newly come, swineherd,
to our house?
sentences.i: “Who, then, is this stranger who has newly come to our house, swineherd?
sentences.n: τίς δὴ ὅδε is 'who, then, is this man here'. ξεῖνος is both 'stranger' and 'guest'. νέον is 'newly', and εἰλήλουθε the perfect of ἔρχομαι, 'has come'. συβῶτα is the vocative of συβώτης. ἡμέτερον πρὸς δῶμα is 'to our house'. This first question asks who he is.

sentences.t:
τέων δ’ ἐξ εὔχεται εἶναι
ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.tr:
teōn d’ ex euchetai einai
andrōn;
sentences.l:
And from which men does he claim
to be?
sentences.i: And of what people does he claim to be?
sentences.n: τέων is the Homeric genitive plural of τίς, 'of whom' (Attic τίνων). ἐξ … εἶναι ἀνδρῶν is 'to be from which men', ἐξ with the genitive giving descent. εὔχεται is 'claims, declares': with an infinitive, εὔχομαι means 'claim to be', a sense different from the 'pray' of εὐχόμενος at line 102.

sentences.t: ποῦ δέ νύ οἱ γενεὴ καὶ πατρὶς ἄρουρα;
sentences.tr: pou de ny hoi geneē kai patris aroura;
sentences.l: And where for him is family and the fatherland’s soil?
sentences.i: And where are his family and his native soil?
sentences.n: ποῦ δέ νύ οἱ is 'and where, then, for him', οἱ being the dative 'his'. γενεή is 'birth, family' (Attic γενεά). πατρὶς ἄρουρα is 'native soil': πατρίς is an adjective, 'of the fatherland', and ἄρουρα is ploughland, here 'soil'.

sentences.t: δύσμορος, ἦ τε ἔοικε δέμας βασιλῆϊ ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr: dysmoros, ē te eoike demas basilēï anakti·
sentences.l: Ill-fated, yet he truly resembles in body a king, a lord;
sentences.i: He is ill-fated, and yet in body he truly looks like a king, a lord;
sentences.n: δύσμορος is built from δυσ- 'bad' and μόρος 'portion, fate', 'ill-fated'. ἦ τε is 'indeed, and yet'. ἔοικε takes the dative βασιλῆϊ ἄνακτι, 'a king, a lord', and δέμας is an accusative of respect, 'in body'. βασιλῆϊ is a dative in -ηϊ for βασιλεῖ. The thought turns on δύσμορος: his luck is bad, his looks are royal.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ θεοὶ δυόωσι πολυπλάγκτους ἀνθρώπους,
ὁππότε καὶ βασιλεῦσιν ἐπικλώσωνται ὀϊζύν.
sentences.tr:
alla theoi dyoōsi polyplanktous anthrōpous,
hoppote kai basileusin epiklōsōntai oïzyn.
sentences.l:
but the gods plunge much-straying men,
whenever even for kings they spin distress.”
sentences.i: But the gods bring low far-roaming men, whenever they spin distress even for kings.”
sentences.n: δυόωσι is a rare form whose sense is not certain: 'plunge' (from δύω 'sink') or 'bring woe on' (from δύη 'woe'); 'plunge' is followed. πολυπλάγκτους 'much-straying' is built from πολύς and πλάζω 'drive off course'. ὁππότε καί is 'whenever even'. ἐπικλώσωνται is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἐπικλώθω 'spin to', the gods being said to spin a person's lot as thread. βασιλεῦσιν is the dative plural of βασιλεύς 'king'. ὀϊζύν 'distress' is the accusative of ὀϊζύς, the noun behind ὀϊζυρός 'sorrowful'. The stop ends Philoetius' speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ δεξιτερῇ δειδίσκετο χειρὶ παραστάς,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
ē kai dexiterēi deidisketo cheiri parastas,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and with his right hand he greeted him, standing beside him,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he said, and greeted him with his right hand, standing beside him, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ἦ καί is 'so he spoke, and', ἦ being the verb 'he said'. δεξιτερῇ … χειρί is 'with his right hand'; δεξιτερός is an older form of δεξιός. δειδίσκετο is the imperfect of δειδίσκομαι, a verb of greeting by a gesture, here the hand; παραστάς is 'standing beside'. καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula 'and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him'. The raised dot introduces a speech that lies beyond this part.
